title: M2-5A Reading — Why People Stopped Having Kids
author: C·E·L Mathayom

slides.title: Thailand is having a problem with its birth rate.
slides.body: Let's read to find out what the issue is.
slides.notes: Greet students. Ask: What do you know about birth rates in Thailand? Do you know anyone with just one child or no children?

slides.title: Why is this lesson important?
slides.body:
• It is about a serious social issue for Thailand.
  • It will help you to answer very difficult questions.

slides.notes: Click 1: show word. Click 2: show context. CCQ: If a country has high fertility, do women have many children or few children? (many)

slides.title: Strategy: Predict
slides.body:
DoPredict the main idea before you read.
WhyIt prepares your brain to understand the text.
HowRead the title. Look at the picture. Ask: What is this about?
slides.notes: Explain the strategy. Examples: title 'Why People Stopped Having Kids' + picture of maternity ward → prediction about birth rates.

slides.title: Try it: Predict
slides.body:
The title is: Why People Stopped Having Kids
Which predictions make sense?
 A book about how to raise babies.
 A problem with Thailand's population.
 A story about a family on holiday.
 Reasons why people don't have children.
slides.notes: Ask students: Which predictions are probably correct? Click to reveal checkmarks.

slides.title: Try it: Predict — Check
slides.body:
The title is: Why People Stopped Having Kids
Which predictions make sense?
 A book about how to raise babies.
✓A problem with Thailand's population.
 A story about a family on holiday.
✓Reasons why people don't have children.
slides.notes: Step 2: checkmarks appear on correct predictions. Options 2 and 4 are plausible.

slides.title: Strategy: Underline key words
slides.body:
DoUnderline the instruction words in the question.
WhyThey tell you what type of answer to look for.
HowFind words like purpose, probably, suggest, mean. Each has a different answer type.
slides.notes: Explain: purpose = main idea of whole text. probably = inference, not directly stated. mean = vocabulary in context. suggest = author's implied opinion.

slides.title: Try it: Underline
slides.body:
Read each question. Which words tell you what to look for?
1.What is the main purpose of this passage?
2.What is probably true about the relationship?
3.What does the phrase "social isolation" mean?
slides.notes: Step 1: Students identify key words. Click to reveal which words to underline.

slides.title: Try it: Underline — Check
slides.body:
Read each question. Which words tell you what to look for?
1.What is the main purpose of this passage?
2.What is probably true about the relationship?
3.What does the phrase "social isolation" mean?
slides.notes: Step 2: Key words underlined. Q1: main purpose = look for overall aim. Q2: probably true = inference. Q3: mean = vocabulary in context.

slides.title: Read the article
slides.body:
Read the article and answer all 8 questions.

You have 10 minutes.
slides.notes: Timer: 10 minutes (600 seconds). Students read the article and answer multiple-choice questions on their worksheet. Walk around and monitor.

slides.title: Check your answers
slides.body:
Let's check how you did.

Swap and mark.
slides.notes: Students swap worksheets. Go through each answer with explanation.

slides.title: Question 1 / 8
slides.body:
Question1. What does the passage say about the number of children Thai women have?
AnswerD — They have fewer than one child on average.
Why?The average is 0.8 children — that is less than one. Option A says "the lowest" but the text says "one of the lowest."
Text"The average woman there has just 0.8 children in her lifetime — one of the lowest in the world."
slides.notes: Point out: 'one of the lowest' ≠ 'the lowest'. Make sure students understand the difference.

slides.title: Question 2 / 8
slides.body:
Question2. What is different about today's drop in birth rates compared to the past?
AnswerA — People are choosing to have fewer children on purpose.
Why?In the past, drops were caused by war, disease, or famine. This time, people are making a choice.
Text"The number of people has gone down before, but always because of war, disease, or famine. This time, it is happening by choice. That is new."
slides.notes: Key distinction: past drops were forced by external events. This one is voluntary.

slides.title: Question 3 / 8
slides.body:
Question3. What is the main purpose of the passage?
AnswerC — To explain the causes and consequences of falling birth rates.
Why?The article starts with the situation, then explains causes (paras 5-6) and consequences (para 4). This is a classic explainer structure.
Text"Why does this matter? Fewer people can mean slower economic growth..." (cause) / "So why are people having fewer children?" (consequence)
slides.notes: Main purpose questions test the overall structure. Point out how the article is organized: situation → causes → consequences.

slides.title: Question 4 / 8
slides.body:
Question4. What is the main point of paragraph 4?
AnswerD — Falling birth rates affect both the economy and people's happiness.
Why?The paragraph gives two types of effects: economic (slower growth, pension problems) and human (loneliness, isolation).
Text"Fewer people can mean slower economic growth. It can also make it harder to pay for healthcare and pensions... But the human cost may be even worse."
slides.notes: Main point of a paragraph = the topic sentence + what it says. Point out 'But' signals a second effect.

slides.title: Question 5 / 8
slides.body:
Question5. What does the phrase 'social isolation' mean?
AnswerC — Being separated from other people in daily life.
Why?The paragraph explains that phones let you stay in your room alone. This leads to less time with others — being separated from people.
Text"Your phone offers unlimited content in your own room. This means less time with others and fewer chances to meet a partner."
slides.notes: Vocabulary-in-context question. Students need to infer the meaning from surrounding text, not just from the word itself.

slides.title: Question 6 / 8
slides.body:
Question6. What is probably true about marriage and birth rates?
AnswerB — Fewer marriages are likely to lead to fewer births.
Why?The article says most people have children after marriage. So if fewer people marry, fewer children will be born.
Text"When people struggle to find love, they marry later — or not at all. And most people still have children after marriage."
slides.notes: Inference question. The text doesn't say it directly — students need to connect: marriage → children, so fewer marriages → fewer children.

slides.title: Question 7 / 8
slides.body:
Question7. What does the author suggest about government payments?
AnswerA — Paying parents is not the full answer by itself.
Why?The author says payments encourage more births, but adds that community support is also needed. Money alone is not enough.
Text"Paying parents larger sums does seem to encourage more births, but no government policy has replaced what community provides."
slides.notes: Author's opinion question. The word 'but' signals contrast — payments aren't the complete solution.

slides.title: Question 8 / 8
slides.body:
Question8. Fernández-Villaverde finishes the article by saying: "This is really the only thing that matters." What does he mean?
AnswerB — Thailand's falling birth rate.
Why?The expert says Thailand's situation is "the only thing that matters." The whole article is about the falling birth rate.
Text"What Thailand is facing is a warning for the whole world. As Fernández-Villaverde says... 'This is really the only thing that matters.'"
slides.notes: Reference question — 'What does this/these/he refer to?' Students must look back at the preceding sentences.

slides.title: Discuss with your partner
slides.body:
Why do fewer people in Thailand want to have children?

What could the government do?

You have 7 minutes.
slides.notes: Timer: 7 minutes. Walk around and monitor. Encourage use of ideas from the text. Elicit some opinions afterward.

slides.title: Questions?
slides.body: Any questions about what we read today?
slides.notes: Wrap up. Ask: What new words did you learn? What was the most surprising fact from the article?
